text: A further praise follows, and Johnson states it with his usual plainness: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). The other dramatists, as he saw them, lifted their persons above the common level of mankind. They lent them sentiments which no living man would utter, and a manner of speech fitted to admiration rather than to belief. Shakespeare declined the practice, and Johnson reckons the refusal among his chief merits. His persons speak as the reader himself would have spoken, had he stood in the same place and felt the same pressure. Their words are taken from common life. They move us because we know them, and know ourselves in them. Nor is this true only where the action is probable. A ghost walks the platform at Elsinore, witches meet upon the heath, and the event lies wholly outside experience; yet the speech of those who witness it remains within experience. The marvel belongs to the plot, while the dialogue keeps level with life. Hamlet questions the spirit of his father as any son might question a thing so dreadful; and Macbeth broods upon the prophecy as an ambitious man would brood upon the promise of a crown.
